sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Gent cut through traffic in its centre in 2017. The circulation plan of 3 April 2017 regulates traffic inside the R40 ring, stops the centre working as a through route and extended the car-free zones [0]. A 2016 parking plan had set new tariff zones, more park-and-ride and more bicycle parking [1]. The low-emission zone has applied inside the ring since 1 January 2020 [2]. By the October 2024 elections VRT NWS described the centre plan as largely accepted, while newer neighbourhood plans in Gentbrugge and Sint-Amandsberg met strong opposition [3]. The Voor Gent and Groen coalition agreement of November 2024 keeps the principles of the inner-city plan but removes the 'knip' in Joachim Schayckstraat and replaces the 'local traffic only' zones around Dampoort and Oud-Gentbrugge with other measures [4]. It also says the low-emission zone will not be tightened and could be abolished if a study cannot show its added value [6]. VRT reported in June 2026 that the study is delayed until spring 2027 [7].

On parking, the agreement announces a 'new parking philosophy'. The first resident card stays free and centre garages are to be kept as far as possible for short stays, residents, subscribers and traders. The city will look for visitor parking along the R40 and will examine concentrating it at Sint-Pietersplein and a possibly extended Zuid garage [5]. From 1 April 2026 Sunday and public-holiday parking became paid in the orange and red zones, and the second resident permit costs €300 [10]. Gent counted 42,300 on-street spaces in its paid zone at the end of 2025. About 400 public-domain spaces disappeared in 2025 for other uses, and paid regimes were not extended in 2025 after expansions in 2023 and 2024 [20]. In 2025, 47 cameras monitored access to the car-free areas and traffic filters, and 192,406 municipal administrative fines were issued, 12% more than the year before [9].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city has just rebuilt its garage pricing. From 1 April 2026 the busiest garages charge a peak rate of €4 an hour on Saturdays and during events, standard rates run from €1 to €3.60 an hour, a cluster subscription lets one pass cover several garages, and the 20% discount on bulk parking cheques ends [11][12]. The city had prepared the overhaul after a benchmark with other cities [13]. Its Mobiliteitsbedrijf managed nine garages with 4,098 spaces in 2025, with 2.13 million entries (up 2.4%) and revenue of €10.5 million [14]. Entries rose at Sint-Pietersplein, Ledeberg and Savaan but fell at Vrijdagmarkt and Sint-Michiels, and Het Getouw stayed very lightly used [15].

The city is shifting visitors to the edge. At The Loop, new flexible tariffs from November 2025 replaced a €12 flat daily rate, and park-and-ride capacity there was to grow from 180 to 325 spaces. A parking tower for 500 cars is planned on Veld 5 Oost by the end of 2029 [18]. The city said in December 2025 that it earmarks €4 million a year for new parking places, that a €15 million tower at The Loop is planned and that two new park-and-ride sites are under negotiation [19]. It had 13 free park-and-rides with 1,793 spaces at the end of 2025 [21]. During the Gentse Feesten on 20 July 2026 the central garages were full by 20:30 and The Loop saw more use [22]. In 2025 the garages renewed their plate cameras and introduced payment at the exit [24], and the city's municipal garages together had 86 charging places [26]. An agreement with Interparking for the Zuid garage under Wilsonplein (1,043 spaces) brought the city €737,478 in 2025 [16].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The city's Mobiliteitsbedrijf runs ten of the eleven garages in our data (6,403 spaces, including The Loop) and Indigo the Dok Noord garage (550 in our feed, with no capacity on the city's page) [17]. Our data put three garages within 500 m of the Korenmarkt (1,290 spaces) and two more within 1 km (967). The city's own capacities differ slightly from our feed, for example Vrijdagmarkt at 632 against 580 [14]. The four central garages Ramen, Reep, Sint-Michiels and Vrijdagmarkt charge up to €3 an hour on weekdays and €4 on Saturdays, Savaan €2.50, Sint-Pietersplein and Tolhuis up to €1.80, and Het Getouw and Ledeberg the least at €1.00 and €1.20 [12].

Occupancy over August to early October 2026 averaged 26% on weekdays and 28% at weekends. The fullest are Tolhuis (60%, 148 spaces), Ledeberg (53%) and Sint-Pietersplein (53%, 700 spaces), and the central €3 garages are busier at weekends than on weekdays: Ramen 62% against 51%, Reep and Vrijdagmarkt 56% against 45% and 41%. The emptiest are Dok Noord (8%), Het Getouw (7%) and The Loop (4%, 2,490 spaces), which the city treats as a park-and-ride [18][22]. Within 500 m of the centre the average is 42%, against 11% for the three garages more than 2 km out.

The data cover the summer holidays and run after the Gentse Feesten, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Gent.
